Katmai (Alaska)
Explore Katmai, a land reborn from volcanic ash, and observe the vivid lives of bears, salmon, plovers and coastal wolves that call it home. 

Everglades (Florida)
As the first national park founded to protect wildlife and ecological richness, the Everglades teems with diverse life above and below water. 

Yellowstone (Wyoming/Montana/Idaho)

Olympic (Washington)
From glacial peaks to temperate rainforests and the rugged Pacific coast, Olympic National Park protects unique environments with rich biodiversity. 

Zion (Utah)
In Zion National Park, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons and the Virgin River converge, sculpting a vibrant landscape and refuge for wildlife to thrive.

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Grave Digger (Black Death) | day 4 of 7
snippet.description:
When archaeologists excavated East Smithfield in London in 1986, they found something unexpected.

The bodies weren't buried randomly. They were laid out in neat rows — perfectly aligned, hands folded, shrouded where possible. Over ten thousand of them. In less than two years.

Somebody did that work. Thousands of times. In November mud. For very little pay. And nobody ever wrote their name down.

This is Day 4 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a gravedigger at East Smithfield — the emergency burial ground the Bishop of London consecrated in November 1348 because the parish churchyards were already full. You sleep in a lean-to shelter at the edge of the site. You eat dark bread before dawn. You dig trenches alongside a man named Walter who has made a private agreement with himself about what this job is and is not, and who has not shared the terms of that agreement with anyone.

The carts come every morning. You lay the bodies in rows, east to west, the way the Christian tradition requires — so that when they rise at the Last Judgement they will face Jerusalem. You fold their hands where folding is possible. You do this thirty times today.

One of them is a child wrapped in a blue wool blanket with an embroidered flower near the corner. Someone sewed that flower on an ordinary day that was not this day.

You notice it. You don't mention it to Walter. You go back to the digging.

Using AI trained on the Museum of London's excavation reports and medieval city records, we've reconstructed what one day as a gravedigger at East Smithfield actually looked like in November 1348.

snippet.title: How do snakes swallow animals so much bigger than they are? - Niko Zlotnik
snippet.description:
Explore how snakes evolved, and find out how their jaw-dropping anatomy allows them to take down prey several times their size.

--

Since slithering onto the scene some 150 million years ago, evolving length and limbless-ness out of their ancestral lizard forms, snakes have diversified rapidly. Their noodly bodies and flexible heads granted them access to novel places and prey. And today, there are nearly 4,000 snake species, spanning habitats high and low. Niko Zlotnik explores how snakes evolved into incredible predators.

Lesson by Niko Zlotnik, directed by Anna Benner.

snippet.title: The missing ingredient in how we learn
snippet.description:
Explore the benefits and challenges of using self-directed play-based learning models in schools. 

--

Before the last few centuries, children around the world spent most of their time learning through play: observing and mimicking adults, roaming their surroundings, and sharing what they learned with friends and family. Many communities and educators still believe play is one of the best teachers we have. Explore the benefits and challenges of using self-directed play-based learning in schools.

snippet.title: ☘️ What Is St. Patrick’s Day REALLY About? | Explained for Kids
snippet.description:
Every March seventeenth, people around the world wear green, celebrate Irish culture, and talk about shamrocks and leprechauns — but who was St Patrick REALLY, and why does this holiday exist?

In this Curious Professors current-events episode, Professor Punzworth explains the surprising true story behind St Patrick’s Day, how a real historical person became the center of a global celebration, and how Irish traditions spread across the world — all in clear, kid-friendly language.

You’ll learn how a boy from Roman Britain was captured and taken to Ireland, how he later returned as a teacher, and how stories about shamrocks, snakes, and legends grew around his life. Along the way, we explore why people wear green, how Irish immigrants helped make St Patrick’s Day famous in the United States, and why cities like Chicago dye their river bright green every year.

By the end of the episode, you’ll understand how history, legends, and cultural traditions came together to create one of the most recognizable holidays in the world. A quick quiz and classroom discussion question wrap it all up!

🧠 In This Episode

✅ Who St Patrick really was and where he actually came from
✅ Why the shamrock became a famous symbol of the holiday
✅ The legend about snakes in Ireland and what historians think today
✅ How Irish immigrants helped spread St Patrick’s Day celebrations
✅ Why cities like Chicago turn their river green
✅ Quick quiz and classroom discussion question at the end

🎒 Perfect for curious kids of all ages, homeschool families, and classrooms learning about history, culture, traditions, and world celebrations — all explained simply and clearly.

snippet.description:
Take a tour of the vast, underground network of the Paris Catacombs, and find out how this 18th century cemetery came to be.

For centuries, Parisians had buried their dead in the Cemetery of the Innocents. By the 18th century, the grounds had become overcrowded — spewing foul odors across the city. Residents worried that it posed a public health threat, and petitioned the government for a solution. But where could they move millions of remains? Stephanie H. Smith explores the vast, underground network of the Catacombs.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt | Day 1: The Farmer
snippet.description:
The year is 1250 BC. Pharaoh Ramesses II rules the most powerful empire on Earth. And every summer, when the Nile floods, his government does something almost no civilization has ever done: it takes hundreds of thousands of farmers off their fields — and turns them into builders.

This is Day 1 of our 7-part series: 7 Days in Ancient Egypt.

Today, you are a farmer. Your fields are underwater. The state has conscripted you to haul mud bricks for the pharaoh's mortuary temple on the west bank of Thebes. You will carry them on a wooden yoke until your shoulders bruise permanently. You will eat gritty bread that slowly grinds your teeth to stumps. Your wife has a disease from the river water that no doctor in 1250 BC can name. And tonight, you will sleep on a rooftop under a sky so full of stars it casts shadows.

This isn't slavery. This is policy.

Using AI trained on archaeological evidence and historical records, we've reconstructed what one day of ordinary life in ancient Egypt actually looked like — not the gold masks, not the pharaohs, but the real Egypt.

snippet.title: Why does Akhenaten appear with feminine features in his statues? #ancientegypt #egyptianmuseum
snippet.description:
Why does Akhenaten appear with feminine features in his statues?

Akhenaten’s statues are among the most debated works in ancient Egyptian art. He is often shown with a narrow waist, wide hips, a soft belly, long limbs, and unusual body proportions.

But this does not necessarily mean this was his real body.

Many Egyptologists believe this was part of the Amarna artistic style, a revolutionary style created during Akhenaten’s reign. It broke away from the traditional image of the strong, idealized pharaoh.

Another theory says these features had a religious meaning. Akhenaten may have been shown as a king who symbolically carried both masculine and feminine creative powers, because he represented Aten, the sun disk, the source of life.

Some older theories suggested illness or hormonal disorders, but there is no clear evidence proving that.

So the most accepted explanation is that Akhenaten’s feminine-looking features were mainly artistic and religious symbolism, not proof that he was physically female or biologically different.

An evil stepmother demands a maiden’s lungs and liver; a girl is ripped from a wolf’s stomach; and sisters mutilate their feet to squeeze into a gold slipper. During the early 1800s, brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm gathered these unflinchingly gory details from stories circulating around what’s now Germany. Claudia Schwabe explores how these now-infamous tales evolved as they spread worldwide.

An evil stepmother demands a maiden’s lungs and liver; a girl is ripped from a wolf’s stomach; and sisters mutilate their feet to squeeze into a gold slipper. Claudia Schwabe explores how these now-infamous tales evolved as they spread worldwide.

snippet.title: What Did Philadelphia Look Like in 1776? (AI Reconstruction) 250 Year Anniversary
snippet.description:
What did Philadelphia look like in 1776 — the year America was born? This AI reconstruction takes you inside the largest, richest, and most important city in colonial America during the most consequential year in its history.

Philadelphia in 1776 was bigger than Boston, bigger than New York, and more diverse than any city in the English-speaking world. With 30,000 residents, over 120 taverns, and the longest outdoor market in the colonies, this wasn't a quiet colonial outpost — it was a thriving, cosmopolitan capital where Quakers, German immigrants, enslaved Africans, and revolutionary firebrands lived side by side on William Penn's original grid streets.

While delegates debated treason inside the Pennsylvania State House, ordinary Philadelphians were living their daily lives just blocks away. This is what that city actually looked like — the cobblestone streets, the printing presses, the slave quarters, and the taverns where the Founding Fathers drank madeira after signing the Declaration of Independence.

In this video, we reconstruct colonial Philadelphia using AI visualization based on historical maps, period accounts, and archaeological evidence:

→ William Penn's grid — the first planned city in America, with streets 100 feet wide
→ High Street Market — the longest outdoor market in the colonies, stretching several blocks
→ The printing capital — at least seven newspapers and dozens of print shops, where Thomas Paine's Common Sense sold 500,000 copies in its first year
→ The tavern culture — over 120 licensed drinking establishments for 30,000 people, including the City Tavern where Adams, Jefferson, and Washington gathered after sessions
→ Slavery in the city of freedom — approximately 1,500 enslaved people lived in Philadelphia while delegates signed "all men are created equal"
→ The free Black community — one of the largest in the colonies, building churches, businesses, and institutions
→ The night watch — men walking dark streets calling out the time and weather
→ The British invasion — Philadelphia would be occupied from September 1777 to June 1778

This is not the version of 1776 you learned in school. This is the real Philadelphia — messy, divided, brilliant, and hypocritical. A city inventing democracy while keeping slaves. A city of taverns and printing presses where the most important document in American history was written, debated, and signed.

2026 marks the 250th anniversary of American independence.

snippet.title: Do imaginary friends make you smarter?
snippet.description:
Explore the psychology behind why children invent imaginary companions and what skills they can develop through pretend play.
